'''''Eucalyptus camaldulensis''''', commonly known as '''river red gum''',<ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew |title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/b81ef7c6-89a0-45d7-9b2b-cebb16c7033a |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Myrtaceae]], and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to Australia. It is a tree with smooth white or cream-coloured bark, lance-shaped or curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven or nine, white flowers and hemispherical fruit with the valves extending beyond the rim. A familiar and iconic tree, it is seen along many watercourses across inland Australia, providing shade in the extreme temperatures of central Australia and elsewhere.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{convert|20|m}} but sometimes to {{convert|45|m}} and often does not develop a [[lignotuber]]. The bark is smooth white or cream-coloured with patches of yellow, pink or brown. There are often loose, rough slabs of bark near the base. The juvenile leaves are lance-shaped, {{cvt|80-180|mm}} long and {{cvt|13-25|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are lance-shaped to curved, the same dull green or greyish green colour on both sides, {{cvt|50-300|mm}} long and {{cvt|7-32|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|8-33|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of seven, nine or sometimes eleven, in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|5-28|mm}} long, the individual flowers on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-10|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to more or less spherical, green to creamy yellow, {{cvt|6-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-6|mm}} wide with a prominently beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] {{cvt|3-7|mm}} long. Flowering mainly occurs in summer and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|2-5|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-10|mm}} wide on a pedicel {{cvt|3-12|mm}} long with the valves raised above the rim.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="Euclid">{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''camaldulensis'' River red gum, Murray red gum|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_camaldulensis_subsp._camaldulensis.htm?zoom_highlight=Eucalyptus+camaldulensis|publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research|access-date=4 March 2018}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~camaldulensis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="efloraSA">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Eucalyptus_camaldulensis |publisher=State Herbarium of South Australia |access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref><ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis''|id=5580}}</ref> The plant's flowers bloom for a long time throughout the year.<ref name="WFO">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000954597 |publisher=World Flora Online |access-date=17 October 2024}}</ref>

The limbs of river red gums, sometimes whole trees, often fall without warning so that camping or picnicking near them is dangerous, especially if a tree has dead limbs or the tree is under stress.<ref name="Parks">{{cite web |title=Tree risk |url=https://parkweb.vic.gov.au/safety/be-safe-plan-ahead/tree-risk |publisher=Parks Victoria |access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' was first formally described in 1832 by [[Friedrich Dehnhardt]] who published the description in ''Catalogus Plantarum Horti Camaldulensis''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455502|publisher=APNI|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="Dehnh.">{{cite book |last1=Dehnhardt |first1=Friedrich |title=Catalogus Plantarum Horti Camaldulensis |date=1832 |location=Naples |page=20 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=chi.14529141&seq=26 |access-date=4 March 2026  }}</ref>

Seven subspecies of ''E. camaldulensis'' have been described and accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]. The most variable character is the shape and size of the operculum, followed by the arrangement of the stamens in the mature buds and the density of veins visible in the leaves. The subspecies are:<ref name="Euclid" />
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''acuta'' <small>[[Ian Brooker]] & [[Maurice W. McDonald|M.W.McDonald]]</small><ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''acuta''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/222978|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has mature flower buds with a pointed operculum {{cvt|6-9|mm}} long and erect stamens and broadly lance-shaped or egg-shaped juvenile leaves;
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''arida'' <small>Ian Brooker & M.W.McDonald</small><ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''arida''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/222979|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has bluish green adult leaves with only a few veins and mature flowers buds with a curved to rounded operculum {{cvt|3-7|mm}} long;
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' <small>[[Frederick Dehnhardt|Dehnh.]]</small> subsp. ''camaldulensis''<ref name=APC3>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''camaldulensis''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/166035|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has a strongly beaked operculum, incurved or irregularly bent stamens and narrow lance-shaped juvenile leaves;
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''minima'' <small>Ian Brooker & M.W.McDonald</small><ref name=APC4>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''minima''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/222980|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has mature flower buds that are small with a conical operculum {{cvt|2-4|mm}} long and broad juvenile leaves that are usually covered with a powdery bloom;
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''obtusa'' <small>([[William Blakely|Blakely]]) Ian Brooker & M.W.McDonald</small><ref name=APC5>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''obtusa''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/222981|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has white, powdery bark in some months and mature flower buds with a curved, conical operculum {{cvt|4-7|mm}} long;
* ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''refulgens'' <small>Ian Brooker & M.W.McDonald</small><ref name=APC6>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. * ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''simulata'' <small>Ian Brooker & [[David Arthur Kleinig|Kleinig]]</small>.<ref name=APC7>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''simulata''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/119625|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> has a horn-shaped operculum {{cvt|9-16|mm}} long.

The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''camaldulensis'') is a reference to a private estate garden ([[L'Hortus Camaldulensis di Napoli]]) near the Camaldoli monastery in Naples, where Frederick Dehnhardt was the chief gardener.<ref name="Euclid" /> The [[Type (biology)|type]] specimen was grown in the gardens from seed presumably collected in 1817 near [[Condobolin]] by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cleland|first=J. B.|author-link=John Burton Cleland|year=1956|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' and ''E. longirostris'' (''rostrata'')|journal=The Victorian Naturalist|volume=73|pages=10–14|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40965502}}</ref> and was grown there for about one hundred years before being removed in the 1920s.<ref name="Boland" /> Herbarium specimen of the [[holotype]] is deposited in the herbarium of [[Natural History Museum, Vienna|Natural History Museum of Vienna]].<ref>[https://w.jacq.org/W0003122 W 0003122] ([https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.specimen.w0003122 mirror in JSTOR])</ref>

Although Dehnhardt was the first to formally describe ''E. camaldulensis'', his book was largely unknown to the botanical community. In 1847 [[Diederich Franz Leonhard von Schlechtendal|Diederich von Schlechtendal]] gave the species the name ''Eucalyptus rostrata'' but the name was illegitimate (a [[nomen illegitimum]]) because it had already been applied by [[Antonio José Cavanilles|Cavanilles]] to a different species (now known as ''[[Eucalyptus robusta]]'').<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus rostrata'' Schltdl.|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454514|publisher=APNI|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> In the 1850s, [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] labelled some specimens of river red gum as ''Eucalyptus longirostris'' and in 1856 [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel|Friedrich Miquel]] published a description of von Mueller's specimens, formalising the name ''E. longirostris''.<ref name=APNI2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus longirostris'' F.Muell. ex Miq.|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455179|publisher=APNI|access-date=4 April 2019}}</ref> Finally in 1934, [[William Blakely]] recognised Dehnhardt's priority and the name ''E. camaldulensis'' for river red gum was accepted.<ref name="Boland">{{Cite book|last1=Boland|first1=D.J.|author-link=species:Douglas John Boland|last2=Brooker|first2=M.I.H.|author-link2=Ian Brooker|last3=Chippendale|first3=G.M.|author-link3=George Chippendale|last4=Hall|first4=N.|last5=Hyland|first5=B.P.M.|author-link5=Bernard Hyland|last6=Johnston|first6=R.D.|last7=Kleinig|first7=D.A.|author-link7=:es:David Arthur Kleinig|last8=McDonald|first8=M.W.|author-link8=species:Maurice W. McDonald|last9=Turner|first9=J.D.|year=2006|title=Forest Trees of Australia|edition=5th|location=[[Collingwood, Victoria|Collingwood, VIC]]|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|page=320|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CRQg11hSJ1kC&dq=Dehnhardt&pg=PA320}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:RiverRedGum CentralAustralia.JPG|thumb|upright|The dry river beds of central Australia have sufficient underground water flow to sustain the trees.]]
''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' has the widest natural distribution of any eucalyptus species. It is commonly found along waterways and there are only a few locations where the species is found away from a watercourse.<ref>{{cite book|url=http://www.publish.csiro.au/pid/7055.htm|title=''Flooded Forest and Desert Creek''] |author1=Colloff, Matthew |publisher=CSIRO Publishing|year=2014|isbn=978-0-643-10919-3}}</ref><ref name="Wilson1995">{{cite book|last=Wilson|first=N.|title=The Flooded Gum Trees: Land Use and Management of River Red Gums in New South Wales|publisher=Nature Conservation Council of New South Wales|year=1995|location=Sydney}}{{pages needed|date=October 2024}}</ref> 
* Subspecies ''acuta'' is common along rivers from south of [[Cape York Peninsula]] in [[Queensland]] to the [[North West Slopes|north west slopes and plains]] of [[New South Wales]] but is absent from coastal areas and the arid inland.
* Subspecies ''arida'' has the widest distribution of the subspecies and is found in all mainland states except Victoria. It grows in arid regions but only where there is sufficient [[subsoil]] moisture.<ref name="Euclid" /><ref name=FloraBase1>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''arida''|id=35344}}</ref>
* Subspecies ''camaldulensis'' is the dominant eucalypt along the [[Murray–Darling basin|Murray-Darling]] river system and its tributaries. It also occurs on the [[Eyre Peninsula|Eyre]] and [[Yorke Peninsula]]s and [[Kangaroo Island]] in [[South Australia]] and in some locations along the [[Hunter River (New South Wales)|Hunter River]] in New South Wales. It is the only subspecies in coastal [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].<ref name="Euclid" /><ref name="RBGV2">{{cite web |last1=Messina |first1=Andre |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' subsp. ''camaldulensis'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/2a8fd3b6-cbb4-48ee-8b82-948eedb8c0e8 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=5 April 2019}}</ref>
* Subspecies ''minima'' is endemic to South Australia, where it grows in the northern [[Flinders Ranges]] and the northern Eyre Peninsula.<ref name="Euclid" />
* Subspecies ''obtusa'' is endemic to tropical northern Australia, including parts of the Kimberley, the [[Top End]] and the [[Gulf of Carpentaria]] hinterland as far east as the [[Gilbert River, Queensland]] in [[Queensland]].<ref name="Euclid" />
* Subspecies ''refulgens'' is endemic to the [[Pilbara]]-[[Gascoyne]]-[[Carnarvon (biogeographic region)|Carnarvon]] region, along rivers flowing westwards, including along some of the tributaries of the upper [[Murchison River (Western Australia)|Murchison River]].<ref name="Euclid" />
* Subspecies ''simulata'' is mainly restricted to some rivers on Cape York Peninsula, but with some populations further south.<ref name="Euclid" />
In Victoria the species is known to hybridise with ''[[Eucalyptus ovata]]'' as ''[[Eucalyptus ×studleyensis]].''<ref>{{Cite web |title=VicFlora: Eucalyptus ×studleyensis |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/8e309ea7-10aa-40a9-a52d-4ba93b1ce194 |access-date=2025-09-23 |website=vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au}}</ref>

''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' grows under a wide range of climatic conditions from tropical to temperate, but the main areas are characterised by 5 to 20 frosts in winter and high summer temperatures. Temperature conditions may vary from a minimum of -6°C to a maximum of 54°C with a diurnal range up to 21°C.<ref name="fao">{{cite web |last1=Turnbull |first1=John Wright |title=The Ecology and Variation of ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |url=https://www.fao.org/4/e4209e/E4209E07.htm |publisher=Forest Research Institute, Canberra |access-date=22 September 2024}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Eucalyptus camaldulensis29099592294 b1652b769b o.jpg|thumb|''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'', [[Edward River]], NSW]]
The species can be found along the banks of watercourses, as well as the floodplains of those watercourses. Due to the proximity to these watercourses, river red gum is subject to regular flooding in its natural habitat. River red gum prefers soils with clay content. The trees not only rely on rainfall but also on regular flooding, since flooding recharges the sub-soil with water.<ref name="Dexter1986" />

The association of the river red gum with water makes the tree a natural habitat choice, indeed sometimes the only choice in drier areas, for other species. The trees provide a breeding habitat for fish during the flooding season, which also benefits aquatic bird life that depend on fish as a food source during their own breeding season. Wilson,<ref name="Wilson1995" /> who examined the management of river red gums in NSW, suggests shelter is provided for fish in rivers and streams by fallen branches from the river red gum. The "[[snags]]" formed when river red gums fall into rivers such as the Glenelg, are an important part of river ecosystems, and vital habitat and breeding sites for native fish like [[river blackfish]]. Unfortunately most snags have been removed from these rivers, beginning in the 1850s, due to river-improvement strategies designed to prevent hazards to navigation, reduce damage to in-stream structures, rejuvenate or scour channels, and increase hydraulic capacity to reduce flooding.<ref name="Gippel1996">{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1099-1646(199603)12:2/3<223::AID-RRR391>3.0.CO;2-# |last1=Gippel |first1=C. J. |last2=O'Neill |first2=I. |last3=Finlayson| first3=B. L |last4=Schnatz |first4=I. |title=Hydraulic guidelines for the re-introduction and management of large woody debris in lowland rivers |journal=Regulated Rivers: Research and Management |volume=12 |issue=2–3 |year=1996 |pages=223–36}}</ref> However, the Murray–Darling Basin Commission has recognised the importance of snags as aquatic habitat, and a moratorium on their removal from the Murray River has been recommended.<ref name="Lawrece1991">{{cite book |last=Lawrence |first=B. W. |year=1991 |title=Draft Fish Management Plan |publisher=Murray–Darling Basin Commission |place=Canberra}}</ref>

[[Tree hollow|Hollow]]s start to form at around 120–180 years of age, creating habitat for many wildlife species, including a range of breeding and roosting animals such as bats, carpet pythons, and birds.<ref name="Wilson1995" /> The dense foliage of the tree also provides shade and shelter from the sun in drier areas.

The [[superb parrot]], a [[threatened species]], is amongst the bird species that nest in the river red gum.<ref>{{cite iucn |author=BirdLife International |date=2018 |title=''Polytelis swainsonii'' |volume=2018 |article-number=e.T22685072A130018368 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2018-2.RLTS.T22685072A130018368.en |access-date=11 November 2021}}</ref>

River red gums contribute to the provision of nutrients and energy for other species through leaf and insect fall. This is especially important to the ecology in areas of low nutrients.<ref name="Wilson1995" /> The tree's preferred habitat of floodplains and watercourses also gives it the role of flood mitigator, which slows silt runoff.

===Weed===
The global weed compendium<ref name=gwc>[http://www.hear.org/gcw/species/eucalyptus_camaldulensis/ The Global Compendium of Weeds: ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'']</ref> lists ''E. camaldulensis'' as a weed in [[Portugal]], [[Canary Islands]], [[South Africa]], [[Spain]], [[Bangladesh]], the [[United States of America|United States]], [[Ecuador]], the [[Galapagos]] and other countries.<ref name=gwc/> The species, while native to parts of [[Western Australia]], has become naturalised via garden escapees and introduction as a [[land restoration|restoration]] plant; they are the subject of weed management programs.<ref name="FloraBase" /> Its ability to tolerate drought and soil salinity, together with its prolific seed production, and capacity to reproduce when very young, mean that it is highly adaptable, and it has been declared invasive in [[South Africa]], [[California]], [[Jamaica]], and [[Hawaii]]<ref name=cabi>[https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/22596 CABI ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' (red gum)]</ref>

===Reproduction and dispersion===
The flower begins as an "invaginated receptacle".<ref name="Brooker1990">{{cite book|last1=Brooker|first1=M. I. H.|last2=Kleinig|first2=D. A.|title=Field Guide to Eucalypts|volume=1 South-eastern Australia|publisher=Inkata Press|year=1990|location=Sydney}}</ref> The [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]], or cap, protects the interior of the flower bud, as the male and female parts develop.
 
The male parts of the flower consist of the [[stamen]], a slender filament, and the [[anther]], two pollen sacs located at the top of the stamen. The anther sacs open into longitudinal slits to release their [[pollen]]. These filaments will extend to encircle the [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]] during flowering.

The female parts of the flower, the [[ovary|ovaries]], are contained in ovary chambers. These chambers are separated from the receptacle containing the male parts by a disc. From the top of the ovaries a structure called the style extends into the receptacle, to form the stigma.

During flowering, pollen from the anthers can fall onto the stigma. This can occasionally lead to self-pollination, although the stigma does not become receptive until a few days after the operculum has been detached by the expanding stamens, and the flower's pollen has already been released.<ref name="Penfold1961">{{cite book|last1=Penfold|first1=A. R.|last2=Willis|first2=J. L.|title=The Eucalypts|publisher=Leonard Hill|year=1961|location=London}}{{pages needed|date=October 2024}}</ref> Fertilisation will therefore occur with other flowers on the same tree or other flowers on a different tree. Insects, birds, and small mammals help in the pollination of other flowers.<ref name="Brooker1990" /><ref name="Penfold1961" />

After flowering, the stamens will detach. The fruit is the part of the flower that remains after fertilisation, which enlarges, dries, and becomes woody. Triangular valves in the fruit will open, dispersing yellow, cuboid seeds. When seeds are shed from a tree, most fall onto the ground below the crown, with some seed carried by the wind and water. Dissemination occurs mostly in spring and summer,<ref name="Dexter1986">{{cite journal |last1=Dexter |first1=B. D. |last2=Rose |first2=H. J. |last3=Davies |first3=N. |title=River regulation and associated forest management problems in the River Murray red gum forests |journal=Australian Forestry |year=1986 |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=16–27 |doi=10.1080/00049158.1986.10674459|bibcode=1986AuFor..49...16D }}</ref><ref name="CSIROwater">{{cite web|last=CSIRO|author-link=CSIRO|title=''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' Dehnh|publisher=CSIRO-Water for a Healthy Country|year=2005|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/cpbr/WfHC/Eucalyptus-camaldulensis|access-date=26 August 2005}}</ref> while natural flooding occurs during winter and spring.<ref name="Dexter1986" /> As the tree is inextricably linked with waterways, seed dispersion would logically be facilitated by floodwater. There is some contention in this theory, however, where the CSIRO describes an experiment that demonstrated seeds were found to sink after only 36 hours.<ref name="CSIROwater" /> It would also seem that as the seeding and flooding do not entirely coincide, it could be inferred that the conditions for germination, such as damp soil and plenty of sunlight, are more important in the continuation of the species than seed dispersal by means of floodwater. Seeding during the flooding season would prevent desiccation of the seed, which is the main cause of a seed's failure to reproduce.<ref name="Penfold1961" /> Despite this apparent evolutionary advantage of the species living near watercourses to avoid seed desiccation, many seeds will be produced within an ''E. camaldulensis'' forest before one will grow to its own reproducing stage. A gap in the forest must be available for the germinated seed to receive adequate sunlight.<ref name="Penfold1961" />

== Uses ==
Culturally, the species is an iconic part of Australia. Its leaves have appeared on Australian stamps<ref>
{{cite book|editor-last=Kelly|editor-first=S.|year=1969|title=Eucalypts|first1=G. M.|last1=Chippendale|first2=R. D.|last2=Johnston|edition=1st|publisher=Nelson|location=Melbourne|isbn=0-17-006221-X}}{{page needed|date=October 2024}}</ref>{{page needed|date=October 2024}} and is widely recognised due to its widespread range. The use of the waterways for seasonal recreation also occurs within the habitat of the river red gum, again due their fundamental link to watercourses and floodplains.<ref name="Wilson1995" />

An image of [[The Old Gum Tree]] was engraved for a stamp in 1936 to commemorate the centenary of foundation of [[South Australia]].<ref name="ANB">{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/stamps/stamp-proc-SA-1936.html |title=Proclamation Tree, SA, ''Eucalyptus camaldulensis'' |work=Australian Plants on Postage Stamps |publisher=[[Australian National Herbarium]] |access-date=10 December 2010}}</ref>

===Population management===
{{singlesource|section|date=September 2024}}
The predilection of the river red gum for waterways has been a successful evolutionary niche. This has resulted in a large population and range for the species, and so it is not considered endangered. Changes in its habitat, however, could be detrimental not just for the tree, but also for species that depend on the tree for their own survival. These changes include grazing, and water regulation for irrigation purposes. For example, grazing reduces the ability of the species to regenerate, as stock eat or trample the seedlings. However, grazing may aid regeneration by removing thick ground cover.<ref name="Wilson1995" />

In regards to water regulation, there are two problems. One is the timing of the water flow, and the other is the minimisation of natural flooding.{{citation required|date=September 2024}}

Regulation causes flooding to be decreased during the winter and spring months, and water more consistently flows during the summer and autumn months. Since the river red gum disperses its seed during spring, regulating the water may affect the species' ability to disperse using water as a dispersing agent, especially in floodplain red gum forests. Natural water run-off can also be affected, leaving some trees permanently flooded due to the build-up of water behind dams, or the permanent water flow. Neither can seeds germinate in constantly flooded areas.{{citation required|date=September 2024}}

Infrequent flooding due to water regulation provides inadequate water to recharge the floodplain subsoils that river red gums depend on. This will result in stunted tree growth, death of existing trees, and poor conditions for seed germination. Lack of flooding in floodplain areas will change the suitability of river red gum habitat as a breeding ground and food source for other species. Indeed, extinctions of some species have already occurred in river red gum habitats in the Murray-Darling catchment.<ref name="Wilson1995" />

It has been recognised since around the early 1980s that managing water more effectively would ensure the maintenance of river red gum habitat. Water management would include the removal of subsidies for irrigation, issuing water licenses, and the flooding of forests in suitable seasons.<ref name="Dexter1986" />
